source.title: QuEST: Stable Training of LLMs with 1-Bit Weights and Activations
source.authors: Andrei Panferov; Jiale Chen; Soroush Tabesh; Roberto L. Castro; Mahdi Nikdan; Dan Alistarh

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures C4 validation loss across model sizes and fits scaling-law functions, but does so for quantization-aware training and precision comparisons rather than reproducing the original dense-model scaling experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports scaling sweeps for QuEST and variants, which are recorded below. Cited results from other papers, kernel speedups, and zero-shot benchmark accuracies are not scaling-law results for the listed versions and are not rows. The loss curves are mostly figures without tabulated point values.
record.test_reason: This is a quantization-aware-training method paper. It uses the Hoffmann et al. parametric law, extended with a precision multiplier eff(P) (Eq. 5, following Frantar et al. 2025), as a tool to compare precisions and methods. It reports its own method's fitted efficiencies and Pareto frontiers. It does not test whether loss follows a power law, whether fits extrapolate, or compute-optimal allocation. Fit quality is shown only visually (Fig. 12), with no residuals or held-out prediction. The main sweep spans 30M–800M non-embedding parameters (about 1.4 orders of magnitude) at a fixed D/N=100. 'Stable scaling law' is the authors' description of QuEST's training behaviour, not a test of the power-law form against alternatives.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that QuEST trains stably down to W1A1 and follows stable scaling laws. They find W4A4 is Pareto-optimal, beating BF16 models almost 4x its size at equal memory, and that 4-bit is optimal in the overtrained regime. Without the Hadamard transform, W1A1 falls below BF16; the authors say the transform improves the coefficients but does not alter the scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains quantized Llama-family models with QuEST and fits a precision-adjusted loss function; it does not reproduce the original dense-model scaling experiments. Its fitting procedure is described as closely following Hoffmann et al.'s setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Precision and Hadamard-transform use change loss and relative performance; the paper also fits additional data-to-parameter ratios and model/precision extensions.

fits_no_version.finding: A Chinchilla-form law with a precision multiplier eff(P) is fitted to QAT runs (30M–800M, D/N=100, plus D/N=25 and 50 for P=2–4). QuEST eff(P) is 0.02, 0.16, 0.43, 0.70 and 1.02 for P=1, 2, 3, 4 and 8 (Table 2). Fit quality is shown only visually.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss under quantized training follows the dense scaling law with an effective parameter count N·eff(P) that depends only on precision.

record.problems: Most scaling-curve outcomes are presented only as plots, without numerical point values or uncertainty estimates. The main fixed-token-ratio model-size range is limited compared with the several-orders-of-magnitude claim; extrapolation to much larger models is identified as future work.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row cap, omitted separate rows for the FP4 and 2:4 sparse scaling curves (Figure 4(a)), the no-HT W4A4 curve (Figure 4(c)), and the additional D/N=25 and 50 fitting runs (Figure 12), plus the fixed-size/compute precision comparisons (Figures 13–14). They are not individually tabulated; the paper describes these as further scaling-law and precision comparisons. Table 1 comparator-method rows are also omitted because they compare QAT methods rather than add QuEST scaling-sweep points.

untested.parts: The power-law form is assumed (Chinchilla Eq. 4/5) and fitted, not tested against alternatives. The range is about 1.4 orders of magnitude in N at fixed D/N, and no goodness-of-fit numbers are given.
No extrapolation test; larger models are left to future work.
Quantized training is not tested as a separate regime for power-law form beyond an assumed-form fit.
Zero-shot results are given at 800M only.

missing.what: Fitted eff(P) values for QuEST and LSQ (QuEST: 0.02/0.16/0.43/0.70/1.02; LSQ: 0.02/0.12/0.32/0.56/0.87)

record.verdict_notes: The Figure 1 caption says 30M to 1.6B parameters, but the text and fit list N up to 800M; the 1.6B model appears only in the kernel benchmarks. The scaling law serves as a comparison instrument for a QAT method, so the reader's limits_scope labels were dropped. Kumar et al. (2024), which this paper compares itself against, would be a closer precision-scaling source.

versions.untested_parts: The reported primary sweep holds the token-to-parameter ratio at 100 and varies model size and precision on C4; it does not independently establish power laws in tokens or compute, nor cover several orders of magnitude in parameter count. Additional data-ratio fits are reported but not individually extracted.
The paper fits scaling functions but does not report a test showing that fits from small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
It compares precisions at fixed model size and training compute, not the loss-minimizing allocation of parameter count and token count as compute grows.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The study is about text pretraining with quantization-aware training; it does not test other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling laws.
Zero-shot benchmarks compare quantization settings at a fixed reported model size; the paper does not test downstream performance scaling predictably with size or pretraining loss.

The paper describes its fitting procedure and compares quantization configurations, but does not test whether fitting choices cause exponents or compute-optimal allocations to disagree, or whether scaling curves bend away from a power law.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: C4 pretraining with QuEST, primarily at 100 tokens per parameter, across the reported model-size and precision sweeps
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports stable loss-scaling curves, but its principal parameter sweep is 30M–800M non-embedding parameters (not several orders of magnitude), and the fixed-ratio sweep does not separately establish scaling in tokens or compute; see P30-1–P800-16 and WO30-1–WO200-4.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: QuEST without Hadamard transform, particularly W1A1
reader_labels.reason: The paper says the no-HT W1A1 result is inferior to BF16, although training remains stable and the authors say the transform changes coefficients rather than the scaling-law form; see NH30-1–NH800-2.
